nodes.content: Build an incremental interprocedural alias analysis that preserves soundness across pointer escapes, indirect calls, and changing function summaries.
requirements: Soundly handle heap objects, pointer casts, recursion, and opaque external calls under documented IR semantics.
After single-function edits, match full recomputation’s alias answers while reducing median analysis latency by 50%.

nodes.content: Use allocation-site points-to constraints, conservative cast/escape/opaque-call effects, indirect-call target expansion, SCC summary fixpoints, and dependency-indexed invalidation.
How should summary dependencies detect newly feasible indirect-call targets when a function edit expands escaped-pointer points-to sets?
Reverse-indexing indirect callsites by function-pointer points-to sets and escape summaries, then re-solving affected SCCs, matches full-recompute aliases.
Index callsite dependencies on function-pointer sets and escape summaries; propagate changes, discover new targets, re-solve SCCs, verify alias equivalence.
Run AliasEdit-120 edits covering escapes, indirect targets, and recursive SCCs; compare incremental alias matrices and latency against full recomputation.
AliasEdit-120 found 3/120 alias-matrix mismatches: initially empty indirect callsites gained targets without indexed dependencies, escaping SCC re-solving.
Index indirect callsites by function-pointer definitions and escape-summary producers, including empty sets, to restore full-recompute alias equivalence.
Register empty-set callsite dependencies on pointer definitions and escape producers; rerun AliasEdit-120, checking alias matrices and median latency.
AliasEdit-120 yielded 0/120 alias-matrix mismatches and 43 ms incremental versus 104 ms full median latency (59% reduction).
Adopt empty-set-inclusive definition and escape-producer indexing: it resolves three alias mismatches while achieving 59% median latency reduction.
Integrate adopted empty-set-inclusive dependency indexing into the analyzer and add AliasEdit-120 regression coverage for indirect-target growth and SCC invalidation.
AliasInc v0.1 delivers empty-set-inclusive dependency indexing, SCC invalidation, AliasEdit-120 regressions, and documented heap, cast, escape, and opaque-call semantics.
How can incremental updates retract stale points-to facts when edits remove indirect-call targets or shrink summaries within recursive SCCs?
Run ShrinkSCC-80 deletion edits against AliasInc v0.1, comparing points-to sets and alias answers with full recomputation.
ShrinkSCC-80 found 0/80 points-to and alias mismatches after deletions; dependency-indexed SCC rebuilding cleared stale targets.
Specify conservative heap, cast, and opaque-call semantics, then validate recursive edit sequences against full recomputation.
Define IR transfer rules, build heap/cast/external-call fixtures, then compare incremental and full aliases across recursive edit sequences.
Using AliasInc v0.1, add IRSpec-1 allocation-site, cast-to-unknown, opaque-call escaped-heap havoc, and recursive-edit fixtures with full-recompute alias oracles.
IRSpec-1 contains executable heap, cast-to-unknown, opaque-call havoc, and recursive-edit fixtures with full-recomputation alias oracles.
Run IRSpec-1 fixtures through AliasInc v0.1, checking expected may-alias edges and full-recompute equivalence after recursive edits.
IRSpec-1: both solvers missed 4/20 required cast-mediated aliases, invalidating full-recomputation equivalence as a soundness oracle.
Does cast-to-unknown discard allocation-site provenance, causing the four missing IRSpec-1 aliases in both solvers?
Cast-to-unknown drops allocation-site provenance; retaining original targets alongside Unknown should restore all four missing IRSpec-1 aliases.
Patch cast-to-unknown to retain allocation-site targets alongside Unknown; rerun IRSpec-1’s 20 expected aliases and incremental/full comparisons.
Patched IRSpec-1 recovered 20/20 required aliases, including four cast-mediated edges, with zero incremental/full mismatches.
Require cast-to-unknown to retain source targets plus Unknown; IRSpec-1 exposed four omissions that the patch eliminated.
Run EditMix-240 single-function edits with adopted cast semantics and SCC rebuilding; compare expected aliases, full-recompute matrices, and median latency.
EditMix-240: zero incremental/full mismatches and 56% median latency reduction, but both solvers missed two expected opaque-call aliases.
Retain dependency-indexed rebuilding, but block soundness sign-off until opaque-call transfer rules recover the two missing aliases.
Extend opaque-call havoc to transitive escape closure, treating pointer returns as Unknown and invalidating summaries when closure changes.
Are EditMix-240’s missing opaque-call aliases caused by unmodeled writes through pointers stored in transitively escaped heap objects?
The two aliases traverse pointers stored in escaped heap objects; transitive escape-closure havoc should restore both without broadening unrelated locals.
Extend AliasInc v0.1 with transitive escape-closure havoc; rerun EditMix-240’s two opaque-call cases and unrelated-local controls.
Transitive escape-closure havoc recovered both opaque-call aliases; all 12 unrelated-local controls remained unchanged on EditMix-240.
Adopt transitive escape-closure havoc and resume IR-semantics validation; both missing aliases recovered, but full-suite soundness sign-off remains pending.
Trace both opaque-call pointer paths, document transitive escape-closure havoc, then rerun IRSpec-1 and EditMix-240 for soundness and latency.
Trace both EditMix-240 opaque-call aliases through escaped heap fields and document transitive closure-havoc rules in IRSpec-1.
IRSpec-1 addendum records both escaped-field pointer paths and specifies opaque-call havoc over transitively reachable heap objects.
Disabling only escaped-field havoc should recreate both opaque-call misses while leaving return-value effects unchanged, isolating the original omission.
Ablate escaped-field havoc on the two documented EditMix-240 traces; compare required aliases with the full closure-havoc implementation.
Escaped-field ablation lost only one of two aliases; object-level closure havoc preserved the other, supporting comprehensive transitive havoc.
Keep both object-level and escaped-field closure havoc: together they recovered both aliases, while field-only ablation isolated just one.
Track per-object escape-closure fingerprints to invalidate affected opaque-call summaries selectively, retaining conservative havoc while reducing recomputation.
Implement escape-closure fingerprints, invalidate dependent opaque-call summaries on changes, then benchmark EditMix-240 alias coverage, recomputation equivalence, and median latency.
Implement per-object escape-closure fingerprints and selective opaque-call invalidation under IRSpec-1; benchmark EditMix-240 alias coverage, full-recompute equivalence, and latency.
EditMix-240: per-object fingerprints missed 3/240 field rewires with unchanged closure membership; full-recompute havoc retained both opaque-call aliases.
Which field-level changes must escape-closure fingerprints encode to invalidate opaque-call summaries when reachable-object membership stays unchanged?
Hash field-labeled points-to edges, including Unknown targets, alongside closure membership; this should invalidate all three missed rewires.
Add field-labeled points-to edges and Unknown targets to fingerprints; rerun EditMix-240’s three rewires against full-recompute aliases.
Field-labeled fingerprints invalidated all 3 rewires; EditMix-240 had zero incremental/full alias mismatches and retained both opaque-call aliases.
Adopt field-labeled closure fingerprints while preserving object-level and escaped-field havoc; all three rewires now invalidate correctly.
Replace membership-only fingerprints with field-labeled edge and Unknown-target hashes; rerun IRSpec-1 and EditMix-240 coverage, equivalence, and latency checks.
Run IRSpec-1 and EditMix-240 with field-labeled fingerprints, checking expected aliases, incremental/full matrices, and median single-function-edit latency.
Validation report records IRSpec-1’s 20/20 required aliases, EditMix-240’s 0/240 incremental/full mismatches, and 53% lower median edit latency.
Audit IRSpec-1 fixtures against the validation report, checking opaque-call return coverage and controls for the 53% latency comparison.
Audit confirmed all six opaque-return fixtures produce Unknown and matched EditMix-240 workloads support the 53% median latency reduction.
